content.comment_body: Hi, I have a [product_name]: [article_no] with firmware [version_no]. I'm using [product_name] software [version_no]. I've tried multiple SD cards, all formatted as FAT32, including buying a new Transcend micro SDHC 8GB. In diagnostics, I get 'Micro SD Card Rear error'. Trying to copy the program to SD card gives 'Card unknown'. Any ideas? Thanks.

The [product_name] can only read SD cards if they are formatted with FAT32, and you should do a full (slow) format rather than quick. I also have the latest [product_name] ([article_no]) with firmware [version_no]. I tried different SD cards: Emtec SDHC 16GB Class4, SanDisk Ultra SDHC 16GB Class 10, and an older SanDisk 2GB—all worked in [product_name].

I don't have Windows, so I tried slow format with Linux, but still got 'Read Error, Card Unknown'. I went to a neighbor for slow format on Windows—same problem. My card is a MicroSDHC; does that matter, or does it need to be MicroSD? Based on what you said, it shouldn't. I'm stuck—did I miss a step? Is there something special required?

I'm not very familiar with Linux, but from what I know, it can't format media with FAT32 natively. You need a Windows PC for that, and be sure to select FAT32—not FAT, FAT16, NTFS, etc. Format slowly, not quick. In my previous post I mentioned that SDHC cards work too.
Hello. What tool or terminal command do you use for slow formatting? If you do it in the terminal, which one: command prompt or PowerShell? Thanks in advance.

I've tried many ways on Linux and can easily format FAT32 usable on Mac, Android, and Windows. Still, to be certain, I had my neighbor slow format it with Windows—it took half an hour—but it's still not working. I'm lost. I don't know what method he used exactly. Any tricks or steps to follow? Could it be a faulty PLC? Thanks for replying quickly.

I use a Windows 7 Pro PC. When I format the SD(HC) card, I disable 'Quick Formatting' and select FAT32 as the file system. That's all I can advise. Do you know anyone with a [product_name] who could test your SD card?

According to manufacturers (like SanDisk), all memory cards come pre-formatted. SD/microSD 2GB or smaller: FAT16; SDHC/microSDHC 4GB–32GB: FAT32; SDXC/microSDXC 64GB+: exFAT; CompactFlash up to 128GB: FAT32; CompactFlash 256GB: exFAT. I use Windows Disk Management to format SD cards and have never had issues. For [product_name], the program must be named LOGO_U_P.BIN for proper reading. To transfer a program, save as *.bin to the SD card in the software, then plug the card into [product_name] and transfer. Alternatively, transfer the program into [product_name], then copy it to the SD card.

@[user_name], your info is correct and helpful. However, it doesn't address the main issue for the topic creator. He's not trying to save a [product_name] program but a [product_name] project. His device reports an unreadable SD card. He only needs to format SD card with FAT32 and ensure it’s 32GB max, which I already suggested. The detail about SDXC/microSDXC with exFAT is not relevant for solving his problem. Note: [product_name] detects inserted SD cards and shows a specific error message. If no card is inserted, diagnostics display: Diagnostics Micro SD card: Card detached.

@[user_name], check Wikipedia for FAT32 for more details. There are different drivers for formatting cards on Linux and Mac. Since you and your friend used Windows PC for formatting (Win7: FAT32 Standard), if it’s still not working, check: set [product_name] to STOP mode when inserting/removing card; ensure card holder aligns with device housing as forced insertion can damage pins; insert card correctly—the pins should be on top when facing the front of [product_name]. Hope this helps.

I think I've tried everything now. Someone mentioned the speed class (C4, C10) could matter—I tried C10 and C4 (8GB), formatted slowly with Windows defaults. Still no luck. I even disassembled the device’s SD reader—no faulty pins. I found a shop willing to test with a new [product_name]. I'll update soon.
I'm having the same issue. New [product_name] with FAT32 SD card not working. Any solutions or suggestions would help. Thanks.

All solutions have already been mentioned: Format microSD card on a Windows PC using FAT32, disable 'Quick Formatting'; max size 32GB; do not use microSDXC (64GB or more); ensure the microSD card is inserted correctly—the pins should point upward.

If it’s still not working: 1) Go to a friend and format the card on their Windows PC (FAT32). 2) If you lack Windows, read the FAT32 Wikipedia article—explains needed drivers for Mac and Linux for proper FAT32. Card support depends on cluster size. Cards up to 32GB formatted as FAT32 in Windows 7 have correct cluster size. Both quick and slow formatting can work, but I use quick and have no issues if the card and holder are fine in [product_name]. Hope it helps.
Using fast format gave me problems with some cards.
I had the same issue—doing a full (slow) format as FAT32 in Windows 10 resolved it for me.
The small chip that holds the SD card wasn’t working properly. I processed a warranty return, and all my SD cards worked immediately after replacement. Thanks to all.
Thank you for the helpful support and explanation.

Sometimes the SD card isn’t readable by [product_name]. Removing and reinserting sometimes makes it work. The socket inside the card holder might have oxidation or dust. If no SD cards work, try cleaning inside with a spray agent like CRC degreaser. If that doesn’t work, consider filing a warranty claim with the device seller.
TF card? Do you mean microSD card?
Yes, they are essentially the same.

Apologies—I forgot to explain my solution earlier. The problem was the device itself, specifically the SD card tray. With a new device under warranty (since the tray is not separately available), all issues were resolved. For your information, Linux can perfectly format FAT32 SD cards usable on many platforms. Afterwards, all my SD cards worked—formatted using Linux or Windows. Thanks for everyone's help.

I had the same issue. After multiple attempts and following all thread advice, I finally removed the tray and discovered bent pins—this was a brand new device, and I never forced the tray. If formatting doesn't help, inspect the pins for troubleshooting unknown read errors.

Hello @[user_name], welcome to the forum. Looking at your photo, the area for card slot opening shows clear tool marks. The card slot usually only gets blocked if the SD card is jammed due to improper insertion, which bends the pins.

I previously used an SD card with no problem for writing programs on the device but lost it. I bought three SD cards (unknown brand), 16GB, and none worked—even after slow and fast formatting. The cards worked perfectly for PC transfers (including saving/loading files from the software), but when inserted in the device, I got 'card unknown' or 'no program on card' errors. The only solution was a brand new SanDisk card 16GB. It seems the device can be picky with certain SD card brands.

From my experience, I've used many SD cards from various brands and storage sizes (2GB to 64GB) and classes without issues. With the 64GB cards, I had to create a 32GB FAT32 partition, but that worked fine.
Except for the issue with the tray (and no bent pins), I had no problem with all cards I tried, as long as they were formatted to FAT32 using Windows or Linux.

Hello everyone, don’t forget to clear the MBR on a microSD card. On Linux, open GParted, select your card, go to 'Device' > 'Create Partition Table' (like msdos), then proceed. Afterwards, format again (or format to Ext2 then Fat32 to ensure everything is cleared). Make sure all operations are completed before proceeding.

analysis.insight_summary: Users repeatedly encounter problems with [product_name] modules failing to recognize SD cards, even after trying various brands, FAT32 formatting, and using different operating systems. Main frustrations include ambiguous error messages, possible hardware constraints like card slot or pin alignment, and unclear troubleshooting methods for SD card compatibility. There's limited clarity around supported SD card formats and how device hardware tolerances affect SD card reading.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect [product_name] devices to reliably detect and read any properly FAT32-formatted SD card, regardless of formatting method or card manufacturer. They value clear error messages and guidance to resolve compatibility, formatting, or hardware issues for successful SD card use.
